title: Rosmersholm with Hayley Atwell & Tom Burke - review
transcript: welcome to one minute theater reviews I'm Paul seven Lewis this is the Duke of York's theatre and I'm here to see Rasmus home Rosner's home by henrik ibsen in a new adaptation by duncan macmillan at the Duke of York's theatre roses home is about wanting change but being held back by the past the political system religion inheritance at the beginning everything is covered in dust sheets in this stately home Rosner's home the wall show signs of flood damage at the lower levels it's murky until Hayley Atwell playing Rebecca West starts pulling the sheets off and letting the light in it's a year since rasmus wife committed suicide in the lake and clogged up the mill wheel that's causing the flood her death raised questions main one being why did she do it Rosemarie is weighed down by his past not only this recent tragic event but his whole inheritance the high walls of Ray Smith's brilliant set are covered in paintings of his ancestors staring down at him and he's expected to keep the line going we are on the eve of an election and people looking to rosna for a lead but his disillusionment with a political system is profound he renounces his natural party the conservatives whose representative is superbly conveyed by Giles Tarara as the likable but ruthless crawl whose views and views women and the working classes with contempt so it seems Rasmus should back the radicals but both sides take against him and they both own newspapers that lie about him so you can see there are many modern parallels Mulder spoken Tom Burke as razmik perfectly conveys the uncertainty that alternates with his passion for Rebecca but the evening belongs to Haley Atwell she's a force for change and she is a force on the stage her performances bravura but always believable however even she her character is dragged down by the past there are many questions and no easy answers in this epson masterpiece but much the thrill - as emotions once constrained begin to burst free nothing lives in is straightforward and naively believing that all you need is truth is a sure recipe for disaster a happy ending is the least we expect epson is famous for his revolutionary realism and in Rick's ins production and Duncan McMillan's adaptation triumph in making the characters in this hundred thirty year old play seem totally real I give Rasmus home five stars a few more thoughts on Rosner's home a quick word of phrase for the producer Sonia Friedman again she's brought a play to the West End that might have been expected to stay in the domain of subsidized venues and although she's used star names from film and TV the stars are stage actors of the highest caliber commercial producers often look for play safe audience pleases but miss Friedman stretches and challenges her audience and rewards them with an evening of extraordinary thrilling theatre Oh spoiler alert and this is a complaint about the publicity material roses home is one of its ins least produce plays although this may change after this powerful production so audiences are unlikely to know how it ends however if they've seen the picture on the posters and adverts they're likely to have a pretty good idea as the play progresses and I think that's a spoiler in itself and while on the subject of the ending Ray Smith's great design has one last coup de theatre as the water flows onto the set at the end if you've enjoyed this review found it useful please subscribe to my youtube channel one minute theater reviews you
